issues.legal_issue: A public corporation created by a central enactment and wholly owned and controlled by the central government is a corporation whose premises fall within the definition of public premises.
material_facts: The premises belonged to a nationalised bank constituted as a distinct juristic person under a central enactment.
The bank’s entire capital was vested in the central government, which also had powers concerning the bank’s management and policy.
issues.conclusion: Premises belonging to a nationalised bank are public premises for the purpose of the public-premises eviction regime.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of public premises in Section 2(e)(2)(ii) includes a corporation established by or under a central enactment and owned or controlled by the central government. A body corporate can be a corporation even without shareholders or members; a public corporation of the newer statutory pattern may have the nation, represented through government, as its symbolic shareholder. The Court relied on Bank of New South Wales v. The Commonwealth and R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, distinguished S.S. Dhanoa v. Municipal Corporation, Delhi, and overruled Oriental Bank of Commerce v. Delhi Development Authority to the extent it held otherwise.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_case and entity_created_by_central_law and entity_wholly_government_owned and entity_government_controlled

predicates.public_premises_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns eviction from premises claimed to be covered by a public-premises eviction regime.
predicates.entity_created_by_central_law: The entity that owns the premises was constituted as a distinct legal person by a central enactment.
predicates.entity_wholly_government_owned: The entity’s entire capital is held by the central government.
predicates.entity_government_controlled: The central government has powers over the entity’s management or policy.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding concerns premises owned by an entity created by central law, wholly government-owned, and government-controlled, those premises count as public premises.

issues.legal_issue: Commercial use of premises does not exclude them from the public-premises eviction regime, and applying that regime to such premises does not violate the asserted constitutional rights.
material_facts: The dispute concerned premises used for commercial purposes.
The premises were treated as public premises, and eviction was sought from a person whose authority to occupy had ended.
The challenge relied on equality, freedom to carry on business, liberty, and directive-principle protections.
issues.conclusion: The public-premises eviction regime covers commercial premises and its application to them is not unconstitutional on the grounds raised.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(e) contains no basis for limiting public premises to premises used for residence. The need for speedy recovery of unauthorisedly occupied public premises applies equally to residential and commercial premises. The Court relied on Hari Singh v. Military Estate Officer, which rejected an attempt to restrict the statutory meaning of premises. It held that the public purpose of making public premises available for use justified the regime and rejected the asserted grounds under Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 21, as well as reliance on Articles 39 and 41.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction under a regime for recovering public premises.
predicates.premises_used_commercially: The premises are used for commercial purposes rather than solely as a residence.
predicates.occupant_authority_ended: The occupant’s authority to remain in the premises has expired or been terminated.

issues.definition: Commercially used premises remain within the public-premises eviction regime when the occupant’s authority to remain has ended.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who remains in public premises after the authority under which the tenant entered has expired or been terminated is in unauthorised occupation.
material_facts: The occupants had entered the premises as tenants under leases.
The tenancies later expired or were terminated, but the occupants continued to occupy the premises.
issues.conclusion: The continued occupation after expiry or determination of the tenancy falls within unauthorised occupation under the public-premises eviction regime.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(g) defines unauthorised occupation to include continued occupation after the authority under which a person was allowed to occupy has expired or been determined. The words covering a grant or any other mode of transfer are broad enough to include a lease under the Transfer of Property Act. The Court distinguished Brigadier K.K. Verma v. Union of India, which concerned an earlier enactment without this express definition, and referred to Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_case and occupant_entered_as_tenant and tenancy_authority_expired_or_terminated and occupant_remained

predicates.public_premises_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns occupation of premises covered by a public-premises eviction regime.
predicates.occupant_entered_as_tenant: The occupant initially took possession under a tenancy or lease.
predicates.tenancy_authority_expired_or_terminated: The authority created by the tenancy later expired or was brought to an end.
predicates.occupant_remained: The occupant continued to possess the premises after that authority ended.

issues.definition: A tenant’s continued possession is unauthorised when the tenancy authority has ended and the tenant remains in the premises.

issues.legal_issue: The public-premises eviction regime prevails over rent-control protections where both regimes would otherwise apply to premises and an occupant whose authority has ended.
material_facts: The disputed premises fell within the geographic and substantive reach of both enactments.
The occupants had entered as tenants but remained after their tenancies expired or were terminated.

The rent-control enactment regulated landlord-tenant relations, while the public-premises enactment provided a procedure for recovering public premises and barred court proceedings concerning eviction of unauthorised occupants.
Both enactments were enacted by Parliament, and the public-premises enactment was later.
issues.conclusion: To the extent the enactments cover the same premises, the public-premises eviction regime overrides the rent-control enactment, and an unauthorised occupant cannot invoke rent-control protection.
issues.legal_principle: Rent control legislation falls within entries 6, 7, and 13 of List III; the public-premises enactment, insofar as it concerns lessees or licensees of premises belonging to entities other than the central government, also rests on concurrent-list powers. Thus, the conflict is not resolved merely by reference to different legislative lists. Both enactments are special in relation to their respective subjects, so the generalia specialibus non derogant exception does not resolve the conflict. Applying the later-law principle, and considering the enactments’ purposes and language, the Court held that the public-premises enactment prevails. Section 15 bars jurisdiction over eviction of unauthorised occupants; the Court considered that provision alongside Sections 14, 22, 50, and 54 of the Delhi Rent Control Act. It relied on J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, U.P. State Electricity Board v. Hari Shankar Jain, Life Insurance Corporation v. D.J. Bahadur, Shri Ram Narain v. Simla Banking and Industrial Co., Kumaon Motor Owners’ Union v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal, Jain Ink Manufacturing Company v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, and the stated objects of both enactments. It rejected the suggestion that the rent-control procedure must first be completed under V. Dhanpal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, because that would confer duplicative protection inconsistent with the later enactment’s purpose.

predicates.overlapping_rent_control_and_public_prem: The proceeding concerns a claim that rent-control protection prevents eviction under a public-premises recovery regime.
predicates.premises_within_both_regimes: The premises and occupation would otherwise fall within the reach of both regimes.
predicates.occupant_authority_ended: The occupant’s authority to remain in the premises has expired or been terminated.

issues.definition: Where premises fall within both regimes and the occupant’s authority has ended, the public-premises eviction regime prevails over rent-control protection.

issues.legal_issue: The fact that an estate officer need not be legally trained does not exclude leased premises from the public-premises eviction regime.
material_facts: The occupants argued that determining whether a lease had ended could involve complex legal questions.
The eviction procedure provided for notice, an opportunity to show cause and present evidence, a personal hearing, and an appeal to a district judge or another sufficiently senior judicial officer.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a requirement that the estate officer be legally trained is not a ground for excluding leased premises from the regime.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory hearing procedures and the right of appeal to a judicial officer provide safeguards; the officer’s lack of a legal-training requirement alone does not remove leased premises from the regime. The Court relied on Maganlal Chhagganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which treated procedural safeguards and judicial appeal as adequate safeguards against a similar objection.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_case and occupant_entered_as_tenant and hearing_and_evidence_opportunity_provided and appeal_to_judicial_officer_available

predicates.public_premises_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns eviction under a public-premises recovery regime.
predicates.occupant_entered_as_tenant: The occupant initially obtained possession as a tenant or lessee.
predicates.hearing_and_evidence_opportunity_provide: The procedure gives the occupant notice and an opportunity to respond, present evidence, and be heard.
predicates.appeal_to_judicial_officer_available: The procedure provides an appeal to a judicial officer.

issues.definition: A leased occupant remains subject to the eviction proceeding when an opportunity to be heard and a judicial appeal are provided, even if the first decision-maker need not be legally trained.

issues.legal_issue: Objections that could be raised in a statutory appeal, and disputed factual allegations of mala fides, cannot be used to bypass the available appellate process in a direct writ challenge.
material_facts: An occupant challenged an estate officer’s eviction order directly by writ petition without appealing to the designated appellate authority.
The occupant alleged mala fides, which involved disputed questions of fact, and also raised objections that could have been presented in the statutory appeal.
issues.conclusion: The disputed mala-fides allegation could not be determined in the writ proceeding, and the occupant could not raise there matters that could have been pursued in the statutory appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court agreed that disputed factual questions of mala fides could not be resolved in the writ proceeding and held that matters available for consideration in the statutory appeal could not be agitated after that appeal was not pursued.

rule.if: direct_writ_challenge_to_eviction_order and statutory_appeal_not_pursued and (mala_fides_depend_on_disputed_facts or objection_could_be_raised_on_appeal)

predicates.direct_writ_challenge_to_eviction_order: The occupant directly challenges an eviction order through a writ proceeding.
predicates.statutory_appeal_not_pursued: The occupant does not use the available statutory appeal against the eviction order.
predicates.mala_fides_depend_on_disputed_facts: The allegation that the eviction action was motivated by bad faith depends on disputed facts.
predicates.objection_could_be_raised_on_appeal: The objection could have been presented to the statutory appellate authority.

issues.definition: When an occupant bypasses an available statutory appeal, a direct writ challenge does not provide a forum for disputed factual allegations or objections that could have been raised on appeal.
